subject: claymationSheepdog
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: sheepdog.
Style: claymation (Aardman).
reasoning:
I'm thinking through the Aardman claymation aesthetic for this sheepdog module—chunky clay textures, bulging eyes, wide toothy mouths, thick brows—and planning how to translate those stylistic traits into code carefully since I won't be able to test it.

I'm settling on a shaggy grey-and-white Old English sheepdog look with fringe over the eyes, a black nose, and an Aardman-style grin with separate upper and lower jaw pieces, then roughing out body dimensions and joint coordinates for the quadruped skeleton—hips, spine, neck, and head positions—to build the rig chain by chain.

Still defining joint chains...

Designing a Gromit-style head: a rounded skull with forward muzzle and separate lower jaw, a large black nose at the tip, and big close-set eyes made from white spheres with pupil dots partly hidden under a fringe.

I'll add thick clay brow ridges as capsules over the eyes for that claymation look. For positioning everything on the head, I'll use the local coordinate convention with named directions (left, up, forward) rather than raw axes to place each feature correctly.

For the shaggy sheepdog fur, I'm planning to scatter tuft-textured cards across the body surface, which means I first need to build the body as a swept shape along the spine chain with a radius function controlling the barrel-like torso width at each point.

I'm thinking the body itself should be mostly covered by fur, so I'll paint it with a base coat gradient transitioning from grey at the hindquarters to white toward the front and collar, matching the classic Old English sheepdog coloring, before layering fur cards on top.

Still writing fur paint logic...

Each card is just four triangles, grouped per texture so textured parts stay cheap, with tint applied per card like a vertex color. For the fringe over the eyes, I'm thinking about building a shaggy card cluster using a frame oriented along the facing axis, with cards hanging downward from the crown to cover the face.

With flow along +Z, hanging straight down means viewed from the front it reads upside down, so I need the tuft drawn root-at-bottom, tip-at-top in SVG space so the hanging flip puts the tip pointing down naturally. Card width runs along X since width sits in the plane of facing axis and flow. For the fringe, I'm placing frames across the brow line at the forehead, hanging down over the eyes with a length around 0.12.

I want the eyes still peeking out, Shaun-the-Sheep style rather than fully obscured like an Old English sheepdog's coat -- so I'm parting the fringe in the middle with wisps, letting the eye spheres bulge forward of the fringe plane. Positioning eyes forward at 0.14, up 0.07, with fringe sitting slightly behind and above so it only covers the upper portion of the eyes like heavy brows, adjusting the fringe length and tip position so it dips down without fully blocking the eye spheres.

Rather than purely wispy hanging cards, I'm thinking the claymation look calls for smooth, blocky solid fur masses -- spheres and capsules for the ruff and fringe blobs -- with cards used only sparingly for tufts, plus some extruded blade shapes for fringe and ear flaps, aiming for that fingerprint-mottled clay texture. Planning the build in sections targeting around 500-600 lines of careful code, prioritizing correctness.

Setting up imports...

I'm keeping the color palette tight since materials are limited to 64 flat colors -- defining nose, tongue, gum, tooth, eye, and pupil tones. For the paws I'm planning white fur with a muddy brown paint blend near the feet, and considering whether this Old English Sheepdog character should wear a red collar and tag for extra Aardman-style character detail.

Fur will likely poke through the collar, so I should exclude the neck region from the fur scatter and instead build an explicit ruff of cards ringed around it.

I'll limit fur scatter to the body spine sweep, then handle the neck separately with its own sweep plus a ring of ruff cards at the base, keeping the collar visible at mid-neck and adding cheek ruff near the head. For the collar itself, I'm thinking red with a small gold tag hanging at front, maybe bone-shaped.

Now I'm setting up the body geometry: defining a head-scale constant, then plotting spine chain points from hips through chest into the neck, and writing the sweep function that varies radius along the chain to shape the rump, body, and chest with fur coloring.

That total length is getting too long compared to a real Old English Sheepdog, so I should shrink the proportions: pull the hips in to z=-0.22 and the chest to z=0.22, bringing the rump to -0.39 and the chest front to 0.42, with the neck starting around z=0.64 and the head centered near z=0.5-0.8 for the muzzle.

Working out the leg attachment points under the shrunken body...

I'll make forelegs slightly bent with lengths [0.21,0.21] so they reach past the 0.405 distance, and give rear legs three segments (hip, stifle, hock) with lengths [0.2,0.2,0.1] bending forward then back for a natural stance.

Now I'm designing a reusable leg-building function that sweeps fur-covered cylinders along joint chains, with thicker radii for the rear and fur cuffs at the joints, so I can generate front and back legs consistently with named joints like shoulder/elbow/paw for the front and hip/stifle/hock/paw for the rear.

I'm setting the front legs to parent from the spine's third joint, placing the shoulder root near the body and letting the "L" suffix mark the positive-X side. For the rear legs I'm working out root and foot positions along with hock-bending limb lengths to get a natural hind leg shape.

For the hind limbs, with lengths summing to roughly 0.49, I realize three segments give four points (hip, knee, hock, paw), so the paw ends up as the tip joint rather than a separate span, with the paw ball geometry added at the end to be hidden by fur.

I'm positioning the paw as a small flattened sphere at the foot end, computing its center height so the bottom barely sinks below ground, and sizing the leg tube to meet it cleanly. Then I'm adding three small toe bumps along the front edge of the paw to suggest clay toes, placed relative to the foot frame.

I'm also planning fur cuffs around the leg joints using a ring of small fur-card tufts facing outward from the bone axis, angled slightly to read as a textured collar at the wrist.

Sweeping the radius down the leg chain tapering toward the paw, with legPaint blending white fur tones into muddy ground color near the base using noise and smoothstep, and planning a grayer tone for the upper hind legs.

For the tail, I'm going with a short stubby bobbed style fitting an Old English Sheepdog, building a small 2-joint chain rooted at the hips with a path curving slightly upward and back, then tapering the sweep radius down toward the tip for a fluffy stub look.

I'm then raising it a bit into a gentle wagging pose, adding a rounded pompom sphere at the tip textured with scattered coat cards in a cross pattern for fluffiness.

Now moving to the head, I'm setting up a head joint parented to the neck with a slight downward-forward orientation, and defining a local coordinate helper so I can place facial features relative to the bone's own forward/up/left directions rather than world space.

I'm placing the skull as a slightly flattened sphere offset forward and up from the head joint, using more segments for a smoother hero shape, then sketching the upper muzzle as a tapering swept shape running forward and slightly down from the skull, shrinking in radius toward the nose.

I should add jowl flaps as capsule shapes at the sides of the muzzle for that classic droopy-lipped look, then cap it off with a glossy black nose sphere (plus a tiny white highlight) positioned at the muzzle's tip, adjusting its z-position to account for its own radius.

Now I'm figuring out the lower jaw: adding a jaw joint parented to the head, then sweeping a wide flat capsule for the jaw itself. For the resting pose I want the mouth slightly open rather than fully closed, so I'm rotating the jaw bone down by about 12 degrees to create a subtle open-mouth look.

For the Aardman-style grin, I'm planning a row of big square buck teeth across the upper lip, fewer and smaller teeth on the lower jaw, a flattened pink tongue capsule riding along with the jaw, and a dark interior cavity piece to suggest mouth depth -- though that interior piece may end up mostly hidden behind the thicker muzzle geometry unless the jaw opens enough to reveal it.

I'm now working through the actual geometry so the jaws don't awkwardly overlap: positioning the upper muzzle and lower jaw with the right vertical offsets and radii so they meet cleanly at a mouth line rather than clipping into each other, and setting up the joint rotation point to open the jaw convincingly. I'm defining the upper muzzle's curve path with its start and end points to match this layout.

Adding a dark interior sweep for the mouth floor, then placing upper teeth boxes near the muzzle's front edge, just behind where the rounded end cap tapers to its tip.

Checking the geometry, the teeth would hang down to about -0.085, but that overlaps the lower jaw's front region when closed, since the jaw extends out to roughly 0.316 in forward position — so the teeth and closed jaw would intersect there.

I think I should simplify to the classic Wallace & Gromit look: four prominent big upper teeth plus two small lower teeth, with upper teeth attached to the head bone and lower teeth to the jaw bone, positioning the lower set near forward 0.30 pointing upward. For the jaw opening, I'm setting a 10-degree rotation pose around the x-axis at the jaw joint, making sure the rotation direction tips the jaw down correctly given how the joint is oriented forward.

I'm deciding to apply all bone poses after every part is attached, since any handles created afterward will still land correctly in the new pose -- there's nothing jaw-specific needing special placement, so I'll just pose at the end. I'm also adding the lower jaw sweep using the jaw bone, then building cheek/jowl lip flaps as small capsules on either side of the muzzle attached to the head bone, colored whitish, followed by bulging white eye spheres placed on top of the muzzle bridge for that classic Aardman look.

Checking the geometry though, I realize the eyes as placed would actually sit embedded inside the skull rather than bulging out like they should -- I need to recalculate the skull's size and center position so the surface lines up correctly with where I want the eyes to protrude from the face.

Now for the pupils, I'm placing small black spheres slightly forward of each eye's surface so they poke out visibly, and angling them slightly inward toward the nose to get that classic cross-eyed Aardman look.

Still shaping the eyelid geometry...

Let me angle the lid orientation so it only partially covers the eye, giving that classic half-lidded Aardman look rather than fully obscuring the pupil — tilting the dome direction so the coverage boundary sits just above the pupil center.

For color, I'll give the lid a dark grey fur tone to match the coat rather than a pinkish skin tone, since these characters are fur-covered throughout. Then I'm adding brow capsules above the lids — small raised, rounded shapes in dark grey to suggest a friendly, alert expression before moving on to the ears.

Now for ears, I'm shaping them as flattened ellipsoid forms hanging at the sides of the skull, scaled thin and tilted slightly for a floppy, drooping sheepdog look, positioned to span roughly the upper-mid height of the head with a slight outward flare.

For fur coverage, I'm planning tufts of cards scattered across the skull top and hanging fringe frames, plus a ring of hanging beard cards under the jaw and cheek ruff cards for sideburns, all needing their own frame definitions.

For body fur, I'm scattering a few hundred tufts across the body sweep, filtering by normal direction so coverage leans downward and back, with card size and lean angle tuned for a swept-back look. Color comes from reading the coat paint once at each card's root, so I need to check how the grey tuft texture interacts with that tint—if the base paint is near-white, multiplying it over the grey fur could wash things out.

For the belly, I'm planning to generate hanging fur like a skirt by sampling frames along the belly path at a specific clock angle, building upward-facing frames at each point, then creating cards oriented to hang downward with their own lean and flow settings.

Confirming frame(f,...) should work since frame has an `at` getter for the point. For the hanging skirt, with lean 180 the card drops straight down from the belly, giving good ground clearance while legs stay visible — that reads as properly shaggy. Now thinking about the side shag pieces.

Adding more skirt angles at 120° and 240° with hanging fur, settling on angles [130, 180, 230] for the side coverage, sweeping the body sides symmetrically. Then planning the chest white bib via z-based coat coloring, and working out the neck fur sweep with tapering radius from the base up to the chest, making sure the joint overlaps cleanly with the body.

Now I'm figuring out the collar as a ring around the neck midpoint, computing the right radius relative to the neck's own taper and closing it with a catmull curve through the ring items, with the neck joint derived from those items. For the tag, I'm reasoning through the ring's angular indexing to find which item sits at the lower-front position so the tag hangs correctly below the throat, landing on item index 6 as the "down" direction.

Now I'm placing the gold tag disc, orienting its cylinder geometry so it faces forward and attaching it to the neck joint via the chain's last joint. Then I'm sketching the bandana as an extruded triangle outline hanging below the collar at the front, positioning it near that same lower ring item but offset forward and down from the throat.

I'm giving the bandana a red base with white polka-dot spots using a spots paint helper for that charming hand-crafted look, and considering applying the same spotted paint to the collar for visual consistency.

Now I'm working out where to position the neckerchief so it's actually visible rather than hidden under the chest fur, thickening the band into a wider loop with a triangle hanging in front, and calculating the exact coordinates where the neck meets the chest to find a spot that clears the fur geometry.

Refining the exclusion filter...

I'll simplify by just excluding fur in a small region near the bandana triangle and placing it slightly larger and higher. For the head, I'm planning a Gromit-style coloring scheme — grey on the forehead and ears, white on the muzzle and cheeks — based on position relative to the head joint.

For textures, I'm thinking through which SVGs actually add character: a fur tuft texture with dark roots and white tips, and skipping a painted eye texture in favor of using actual sphere geometry for robustness. I'm also considering adding a dog tag texture, maybe bone-shaped with an engraved name, to round out the 5-12 texture target.

For the tag I'm settling on a gold circle with a paw print rather than text. And for a clay/fingerprint effect, instead of trying to tile a thumbprint, I'm adding subtle lumpy noise-based ripples to the coat paint for a sculpted feel.

I'm keeping the eyes as flat white spheres with a black dot in classic Aardman style, skipping any iris detail. For the nose I'll add two small dark ellipsoid nostril shapes, and I'm deciding to skip extra texture for the mouth, bone prop, and tongue midline since they're not essential to the brief.

Now I'm settling on the texture set: a long shaggy fringe/lock shape for fur tufts, a short tuft for the body, plus tags and spots for the bandana design. Writing SVG code...

Still writing SVG code...

I'm placing the tag texture on a plane positioned at the front of the tag cylinder. For the remaining pieces, I'm planning separate part calls for teeth, and fur rings on each leg—roughly two rings per leg across four legs.

Now I'm thinking about the Aardman-style grin: a wide muzzle with dark smile-line sweeps curving from the mouth corners back toward the cheeks, using thin catmull-curve sweeps rigged to the head bone so the lip corners read as a big grin despite the jaw gap.

To seat the smile lines properly on the muzzle's curved surface, I'll drape the catmull path onto the muzzle sweep so it hugs the nearest surface point with a slight lift, then sweep a thin dark tube along that draped path for the smile line itself. I'm keeping the muzzle rigged to the head bone while treating the lower jaw as a separate piece.

No whiskers needed for this aardman-style dog, but I'm thinking through the beard: hanging fur frames dangling from points under the chin along the jaw's underside, explicitly bound to the jaw bone so they move rigidly with it rather than snapping to the nearest joint by default.

Working out nine beard frame positions across the jaw width and depth, sizing them small with a downward hanging flow — the beard will droop down to around chin level, overlapping the chest for a shaggy look, which feels right. Now I'm positioning fringe frames along an arc over the eyes, calculating the forward and upward coordinates based on the skull's curvature to figure out where the top-of-head fringe should sit.

I'll settle on lean 160, tilting slightly forward toward the flow direction. Checking the fringe placement at forward 0.16: it should hang from up 0.185 down to around 0.055, fully covering the eye tops positioned at up 0.15.

Working through root positions so the fringe avoids covering the eyes directly — keeping roots to the outer sides at l≈±0.12-0.14 while leaving the central band near the eyes clear, or alternatively pulling the fringe strands behind the eyes at forward 0.1 with a steeper lean so they shield the brow area without blocking vision.

I'll skip the toe cones and keep simple sphere toes. For rear legs, I'm adding a thigh bulge mass with fur scattered on it for the haunches, and a smaller fur ring at the front shoulder/elbow, then setting up the naming convention for the leg chains across both sides.

Now I'm working out the hind and front leg chains: positioning root and target joints for each limb, picking segment lengths that sum to more than the actual distance so the limbs remain reachable, and defining bend hints so the three-segment legs fold correctly at the inner joints.

I'm sweeping paint along each leg chain with a tapering radius function, and placing a scaled sphere for the paw just above the ground so it doesn't clip through.

For the toes, I'm adding three small spheres across the front of each paw with a slight arc so the middle one sits forward, using the same mud-colored paint and checking that the paw's bottom edge sits exactly at ground level.

For the body, I'm sweeping the spine chain to form the torso and rump, making sure the tail root nests inside the rear dome, then scattering fur cards across the body surface with randomized size and lean for a natural coat texture.

Now I'm working out a belly skirt path and a coloring gradient along the body's z-axis, blending grey at the rear to white toward the front, with matching tones for the head, neck, legs, and tail to keep the coloring consistent across the whole creature.

Still writing shading helpers...

I'm defining a separate headPaint function with its own grey/white blend based on vertical position, with ears getting a flat grey cel-shaded treatment. I'm double-checking that the paint function's return type works correctly as an RGB color input.

Now I'm sketching out the overall build structure: creating a builder named "sheepdog", setting up a seeded RNG, defining metadata with a name and description, and starting to lay out the skeleton joints beginning with the hips as the spine root.

For the spine chain, I'm using a catmull curve with four points producing three spans, naming the joints spine1 through spine3 and parenting them to hips. For the neck, I'm using a shorter catmull curve with two spans named neck1 and neck2, parented off the end of the spine even though the positions don't perfectly align along the z-axis, which I'm treating as acceptable.

Now I'm adding the head joint parented to the end of the neck chain, then defining a jaw joint positioned relative to the head using local coordinates. I'm writing a helper function that converts forward/up/left offsets into head-local space, being careful to handle negative "left" values by switching to a "right" offset instead since the local-coordinate implementation may not accept negative left values directly, then starting to build the skull part.

Building the skull geometry, neck sweep, and muzzle sweep...

I'll add a small highlight sphere near the surface of the nose, then work out the nostrils as slightly lighter dark ellipsoids against the black nose base.

For the lips and jowl flaps I'm using capsule shapes per side, then positioning the eyes symmetrically with a signed helper for left/right, giving each eye a partial sphere shape with a white color and a smaller pupil sphere placed at the eye center.

Still writing eye geometry...

Testing a less steep tilt direction [0,1,-0.7] shows the lid plane just barely grazing the pupil's top edge at the front pole, covering about 30% of the eyeball from the front view — that feels right, so I'll go with this tilt and nudge the pupil position slightly lower-center.

Now checking the brow placement: computing whether the brow capsule actually sits on the skull surface near the eye socket, I find the point is way outside the skull ellipsoid (ratio ~1.7 instead of ≤1), meaning the brow is floating in space rather than resting against the head. I need to recompute the skull surface extent at that forward position so I can anchor the brow correctly over the eye.

Checking the depth of eye penetration into the skull, I realize the eye only sits partially inside — only about 0.035 of its radius overlaps, meaning it would mostly protrude. I want roughly half the eye exposed, so I'm testing pushing the eye position further forward to f=0.2 to get better placement.

Working through it, f=0.2 gives the eye protruding 0.037 out of its 0.05 radius, which is close to half-exposed — a good googly-eye look. I'm settling on eyes at f=0.2, pupils slightly further at f=0.234, and highlights at f=0.254, then checking how this aligns with the muzzle's position and top curve so the eyes sit properly above it without overlapping awkwardly.

Checking placement, the eyes end up sitting close together on top of the muzzle bridge, Wallace-and-Gromit style, so I'll nudge the width in slightly to l=0.065 for that tight-set look. For the brow, I'm testing a capsule shape over the lid and find it floats just outside the skull surface by a small margin, but since it sits above the lid line anyway, it should still read fine visually.

Now shortening the brow capsule so it rests directly on the lid and bridges inward toward the skull. Then for the fringe, I'm computing where hair roots anchor on the skull dome using a radial falloff formula based on forward position and lateral offset, deriving frame points across the skull top so the fringe falls naturally down the forehead and behind the eyes.

Extending the roots forward about 0.1 with a slight downward curl gives a classic bangs overhang above the eyes, letting them peek out below. I'll keep the brow lines positioned lower so they're not hidden by the bangs.

Working out the tip direction puts the fringe drooping just over the eyes without fully blocking them—sitting slightly behind the eye surface but above the eyelid line. Since the cards face along the flow axis with width along x, viewing from the front shows the full card as intended.

Checking the lean/bend logic again: lean tilts the card from the facing axis toward flow, with 0° straight out and 90° lying flat along the surface pointing downstream, which matches what I want for the fringe. I'll apply the same frame-up orientation for top fur, and for hanging beard-style cards a 180° lean with flow along z should still read correctly from the front, just inverted top-to-bottom, which is fine for that effect.

For the cheek ruff, I'm scattering points across the skull sides but need a filter to exclude the front region near the eyes—comparing surface height against a threshold around where the eye front sits.

Now I'm working out the back-half skull coverage for fur using a local z-coordinate filter, then sizing and placing ear geometry as ellipsoids with specific scale and rotation so the ear root sits correctly against the skull's curved side surface, checking that the skull radius at the ear's position is large enough to contain the ear base.

I'm rotating the ear outward by tilting about the z-axis based on side (left/right), then planning hanging fringe cards along the ear's bottom edge, spacing roughly five across the ear's width.

Now I'm placing those fringe cards with tinted grey paint color and sizing, then moving on to a neck ruff made of outward-drooping ring cards at the shoulders and a second ring behind the head.

I'm setting up two neck rings using the chain's tangent-aligned frame—a looser one near the shoulders and a tighter one near the chin—plus a collar ring at the midpoint, then starting to think about hip rings for the body.

For the tail, I'm building a three-point catmull spline running from the rump outward and upward, parented to the hips, with a sweep that tapers thickness along its length. At the tip I'm adding a small pompom sphere in grey coat color with scattered cards for texture, and checking that the tail's starting position sits properly inside the rump dome rather than poking through it.

Now I'm moving to the bandana: defining a triangular outline with a sharp bottom corner, then extruding it with an orientation so the thickness faces forward and the shape hangs naturally down the chest, following the slope of the body's front surface. I'm positioning it at the collar point near the bottom of the neck.

For placement, I need the front-center point of the neck ring, so I'm estimating the neck path's position and tangent direction at the midpoint to figure out where the triangle's top edge should sit, roughly around (0, 0.62, 0.45), accounting for the neck's forward tilt.

Comparing that to the chest surface depth there, the collar ring at the front bottom is actually embedded inside the chest/neck geometry since the neck tube radius and collar ring radius nearly match at that point. So the collar would really only be visible rising above the neck's upper sides, not at the very front bottom.

Checking the triangle's position against the chest surface lower down, I find a small 0.06 floating gap at z=0.49, so I should tilt the triangle backward to close that gap.

Trying tilt [0,1,0.3] instead gets close enough to the chest surface value, so I'll settle on that and exclude chest fur from the overlapping region near the center. Now I'm moving on to defining the bandana placement itself.

Tag radius set to 0.032, positioned slightly forward of the triangle. Now I'm double-checking overall proportions: body center at y=0.5 with belly bottom around 0.3, head height 0.8 at z=0.5, making sure the full bounding box feels balanced.

Working through total length: skull top reaches about 1.0 plus fur tufts to 1.05, while body length spans from tail pom at -0.61 to nose tip at 0.85, giving roughly 1.46m overall. Comparing to a real Old English Sheepdog (shoulder height ~0.6, head top ~0.85), this build is chunkier and more big-headed, leaning into that stylized Aardman-type proportion.

Checking the body radius, rump at -0.39 to chest at 0.44 gives a body length of 0.83, which seems fine. Now I'm calculating the positions of the teeth and mouth interior relative to the head's local coordinates, working out the muzzle cross-section at various points along its length to figure out where the upper teeth boxes should sit, their width spacing, and thickness so they tuck neatly into the rounded front of the muzzle.

For the upper teeth I'll use four across with slightly varied widths, keeping the outer ones shorter, and place small lower teeth boxes on the jaw further back. Checking clearance, the lower teeth tips would normally poke into the muzzle interior but stay hidden, and once I account for a 12-degree jaw-open rotation, the lower jaw drops enough to clear the upper teeth without collision.

For the tongue, I'm modeling it as a capsule bone to the jaw sitting inside the mouth, then deciding to extend it forward into a lolling tip using a catmull path with a tapering radius so it droops out past the lower jaw's front edge for a cute visible detail when the mouth opens.

Now I'm adding a dark interior sweep for the mouth cavity using a thin elliptical radius so it sits hidden inside the jaw volume but peeks out as a dark strip at the top when open, then starting on the jowl flaps as tapered capsules along the upper lip sides.

I'm checking the muzzle width so the jowl capsules puff out slightly past the jaw edge for a fuller cheek look, skipping separate cheek tufts and fur since this is a smooth clay muzzle. For facial hair I'm placing small hanging moustache cards near the upper lip corners, though I'm noting they might end up overlapping the mouth sides and need repositioning.

I'm adjusting the jowl card placement outward so they frame the jaw without blocking the front teeth, keeping their size modest, and deciding to explicitly set a head bone reference for cards that sit ambiguously between the jaw and head. I'm also confirming mud stays limited to the paws, skipping bandana knots and chest bib details, and assigning the coat color versus head paint color per card group before working out the per-call rendering options.

Now I'm working through the leg fur rings: placing clusters at the elbow and wrist points along each leg chain, tuning their count, radius, and card size with a slight lean and downward flow, and distinguishing front-leg white paint from hind-leg grey-to-white paint depending on where the paint value samples along the body. I'm checking that the ring orientation follows the chain point's tangent direction correctly, then moving to haunch geometry—placing a partial sphere for the rear hip with coat-colored scatter cards filtered by surface normal, tied to the hip joint bone, before considering whether to add a front shoulder muscle bulge as well.

After confirming part counts and triangle budgets stay well within limits, verifying that the scale option on parts accepts vector arrays, and resolving naming conventions for left/right leg joints and mud coloring, I'm now starting to write out the final TypeScript code, importing the builder utilities and defining color constants for the coat shading.

Still writing color and shading helpers...

Writing head paint logic...

Still defining fur shading...

Now I'm setting up the texture SVGs for tufts and fringe locks, making sure gradients and viewBoxes are defined properly for each element, and sketching the curved path shapes for the fringe locks.

I'm also thinking through the gold tag shape and paw pad with toes, then counting textures against the Aardman-style requirement of 5-12 — I only have a few so far and should add more like an eye highlight or fur-stain blush detail.

Deciding against extra decals like a bone shape, bandana pattern, or nose shine since extrusion can't map textures that way — settling on 3 textures plus 8 paint colors as sufficient. Now writing the body sweep function that defines the dog's torso shape along the spine curve, varying the radius over the parameter t, and setting up the fur filter logic with typed hit detection for the rendering pass.

Writing fringe/skirt generation along the body at three clock angles, building frames and cards rooted at the belly surface that hang downward with varying sizes — then moving into defining the legs structure.

For each side (left/right) I'm computing front limb points with mirrored x-coordinates and bend directions, then creating a front leg chain parented to the spine with named joints (shoulder, elbow, wrist, paw) labeled per side.

Rear legs follow the same naming pattern (hip, knee, hock, paw per side), and I'm applying tapered sweeps along each limb chain for the leg geometry, with paw spheres positioned and scaled at each limb's tip joint.

Adding toe spheres...

Defining the hind leg joint chain...

I'm placing the haunch sphere at the hip position with scale that makes the thighs bulge outward beyond the body's half-width, checking that it visually reads as muscular. The rear leg root sits nicely inside the haunch, so that connection looks right.

Now I'm confirming the front leg attaches to the correct spine joint, then moving on to decorative cards scattered on the haunches and finishing the face ornamentation before assembling the head hierarchy. I need to make sure the bite/mouth function is defined after the head joint exists, and I'm checking the neck's taper and coat coloring so it reads white near the skull.

Writing fringe root positions...

I'm positioning the fringe frames to face upward, assigning them to the head bone since there's no dedicated bone there, and setting up two staggered rows with different sizes and lean angles for a layered look. I verify the math for the frame height at the outer fringe points works out correctly, then move to scattering skull-top fur using similar tufted cards colored to match the head paint, followed by the neck ruff and a pom for the tail tip.

For the collar, I'm building a ring of points around the neck chain and sweeping a tube through them with a closed catmull-rom curve to form the bandana band, confirming that the ring and chain interfaces are compatible with the sweep function. Then I start extruding a triangular bandana shape positioned at the neck with a sharp point at the bottom tip.

I'm thinking through type issues with mixing coordinate pairs and a "sharp" corner marker in the same array, deciding to skip explicit type annotations and let TypeScript infer types contextually from the inline call rather than importing an OutlinePoint type, and opting to rely on bevel instead of smoothing for the corner treatment.

I'm verifying the triangle geometry against the chest's actual width at that height to confirm the bandana shape fits properly, checking which bone/joint it should attach to for riding on the neck correctly, and computing the tag's z-position along the chest curve by projecting onto the normalized direction vector and adjusting for mesh thickness.

Still positioning the tag geometry...

For the mouth, I'm draping a smile curve along the muzzle surface using catmull-rom points and sweeping a thin tube along it with rounded caps in the mouth color.

Now I'm checking that the smile line lands correctly on the muzzle's sides near the bottom edge, then moving on to add the eyeballs as sphere geometries attached to the head bone with a slightly yellowed clay-white color.
